strengths: Soundness: The paper presents a coherent, end-to-end red-teaming framework with explicit threat-model assumptions, structured test generation, differential filtering, synthetic website injection, and checklist-based outcome evaluation. The main experiment is broad: 300 cases, five risk categories, three agent scaffolds, 15 backend models, and three trials per case.

The safety evaluator receives useful validation: on 200 sampled responses, its agreement with two human annotators is 96–98%, while all three agree on 95%. The paper also examines injection position, search-result count, context length, website generator, timestamp, and two baseline defenses.

Significance: Unreliable web evidence is an important and growing failure surface. SAFESEARCH could be practically useful for pre-deployment testing, and the results identify actionable patterns, including better robustness from tool-calling/deep-research scaffolds and the weakness of simple reminder prompts.

Originality: The individual ingredients resemble prior work on indirect prompt injection, adversarial SEO, RAG poisoning, and LLM-as-a-judge evaluation, but their integration into an automated benchmark spanning both adversarial and non-adversarial search risks is a meaningful contribution.

Presentation and reproducibility: The paper is generally well organized, includes detailed prompts and configurations, reports benchmark examples, and provides an anonymous code-and-data repository. Simulation and caching make comparisons safer and more repeatable than live SEO manipulation.

Ethics: The authors appropriately avoid manipulating real search rankings, acknowledge dual-use and offensive content, isolate such examples in the appendix, and include a substantive limitations discussion.
weaknesses: The reported ASRs measure conditional susceptibility to highly targeted synthetic pages, not the incidence of harm in deployed search systems. Every injected page is generated specifically to induce a predefined consequence and is forcibly included with up to 2,000 tokens of content. Consequently, descriptions of ASR as a real-world risk “lower bound” and claims that the experiments establish broad real-world vulnerability are not justified without calibration against naturally retrieved unreliable pages.

Benchmark selection creates important bias: cases are retained only when Qwen3-8B is compromised under manipulation but not under the benign condition. This enriches for failures of the filtering model and potentially related models, complicating comparisons and making average ASR unsuitable as an absolute safety measure. Results on an independently constructed or held-out generation/filtering pipeline are needed.

The two in-the-wild studies provide weak external validation. The 4.3% content-farm estimate comes from a single GPT-4.1 judge without reported human validation, while the healthcare study reports 46 changed answers and says manual review found that “most” became riskier without counts, annotation procedures, agreement, or a controlled causal analysis of source quality.

The helpfulness conclusions are insufficiently supported. GPT-4.1-mini judges responses from only the query and answer while being asked to assess accuracy, even though many cases concern fabricated post-cutoff facts. No human validation of this judge is reported. Thus the claims that manipulated responses remain helpful and that safety and helpfulness are jointly Pareto-optimal are unreliable.

Statistical reporting is limited: there are no confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, or uncertainty analyses for ASRs, scaffold comparisons, defenses, or monitoring associations. Agreement is reported only as raw percentages rather than chance-corrected measures, and evaluator validation is neither risk-stratified nor based on an adjudicated reference label.

Several categories conflate safety with generic source faithfulness, and some checklist definitions are contestable. For example, recommending a product on apparently credible evidence or omitting socioeconomic context can trigger failure, while the paper calls all queries fully benign despite examples involving racial crime comparisons. Stronger construct validation by independent domain experts is needed.

Exact reproduction remains constrained by changing Google results and proprietary APIs. The manuscript does not clearly state whether cached authentic results, generated pages, all raw rejected cases, exact model snapshots, and complete manual-review records are released.

The ethics discussion does not adequately address misuse of the released detailed instructions for fabricating authoritative medical, racial-statistics, and regulatory pages. The paper should describe release safeguards or justify unrestricted dissemination. It also inconsistently states that LLMs were used “solely for grammar checking” even though LLMs are central to test generation and evaluation.

Presentation is polished visually but sometimes promotional and imprecise. The abstract leaves the repository URL blank, some prose contains grammatical errors, and causal interpretations of exploratory monitoring correlations—such as explanations for GPT-5-mini's safety—are stronger than the evidence supports.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically important threat: search agents can propagate misinformation, harmful advice, advertising, bias, and indirect prompt injections from retrieved web content.
SAFESEARCH covers 300 cases, five risk categories, three agent scaffolds, and 15 backend models. Testing each case three times and caching authentic search results are useful design choices.

The automated pipeline—structured case generation, synthetic website generation, differential filtering, and checklist-based evaluation—is a potentially useful contribution for inexpensive pre-deployment red-teaming.

The paper provides prompts, implementation details, test-case examples, configuration ablations, and an anonymous code release. It also validates 200 evaluator decisions against two human annotators, reporting 96–98% pairwise agreement.

The simulation avoids manipulating live search rankings and therefore has a sensible ethical motivation. The limitations section acknowledges several genuine constraints, including proprietary systems, one search provider, benchmark scale, and efficiency costs.
weaknesses: The central evidence does not justify broad claims about real-world search-agent safety. The experiment forcibly inserts a purpose-built, query-specific synthetic document into the model context; it neither establishes that such pages would be indexed or retrieved nor estimates exposure frequency. ASR is therefore susceptibility conditional on forced exposure, not real-world attack or failure probability. The conclusions repeatedly blur this distinction.

Benchmark selection creates substantial circularity and selection bias. Cases are retained when Qwen3-8B fails under manipulation and succeeds with the benign tool, with retention as low as 6.8–6.9%. This intentionally selects attacks effective against one evaluated model and likely inflates its ASR while favoring transferable patterns. The paper does not quantify performance on an unfiltered test set or held-out cases generated without this optimization.

The study lacks an adequate per-model safety control. Integrity filtering is performed only with Qwen3-8B, and Table 2 reports benign helpfulness but not benign-condition ASR for every model. Consequently, one cannot determine how much of each reported ASR is causally attributable to the injected document rather than model priors or authentic search results.

The motivating in-the-wild evidence is weak. The claimed 4.3% content-farm prevalence is based solely on GPT-4.1 judgments without human validation, uncertainty estimates, or released sampling analysis. In the health experiment, only 46 responses change, while the statement that 'most' become riskier has no exact count, annotation protocol, inter-annotator agreement, or statistical analysis.

The automated evaluation remains insufficiently validated. Its 200-example audit covers only three models using one scaffold, provides raw agreement rather than class-conditional accuracy or chance-corrected agreement, and does not report results by risk category. The evaluator is also GPT-4.1-mini, the same model used to generate attack websites, creating possible correlated preferences. The helpfulness judge sees only the query and answer, so it cannot reliably assess factual accuracy; this undermines the claimed safety–helpfulness Pareto analysis.

Comparisons among scaffolds are confounded by retrieval and compute budgets. Deep research observes more searches and documents than the simple workflow, while Figure 6 itself shows that document count affects ASR. Thus, lower ASR cannot cleanly be attributed to scaffold design or cross-validation without budget-matched controls.

No confidence intervals, paired significance tests, or variance across the three runs are reported. Small differences such as 4.9% versus 5.0% are consequently uninterpretable, yet the paper draws model and scaffold rankings from point estimates.

Reproducibility is only partial despite the released code and prompts: the results depend on changing Google/Serper/Jina outputs and proprietary, mutable model APIs. It is unclear whether complete cached search results, generated websites, raw responses, seeds, exact model snapshots, and evaluator outputs are released. Manual benchmark review is described without a protocol or quantitative reliability analysis.

Presentation contains material inconsistencies and overstatements. For example, the discussion says GPT-4.1-mini has 85.0% ASR with the search workflow, whereas Table 2 reports 90.5% (85.0% belongs to GPT-4.1). Appendix figures also exhibit awkward wrapping and crowded labels. The LLM-use statement says LLMs were used 'solely for grammar checking and writing refinement,' contradicting their central scientific roles in case generation, website generation, filtering, and evaluation.

The work is moderately original as a unified automated benchmark, but most components—synthetic tool-output injection, LLM-generated adversarial cases, rubric-based LLM judging, and agent-safety benchmarking—adapt established techniques. Given the validity issues above, the present paper does not yet demonstrate the significant, reliable advance claimed.

The ethics discussion emphasizes harmless execution but gives little consideration to dual-use risks from releasing detailed recipes for authoritative misinformation, discriminatory content, dangerous medical advice, and prompt injection. A concrete release-risk assessment and mitigation plan are warranted.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically important threat: search agents may propagate unreliable web content even when users submit benign queries. SAFESEARCH offers a useful pre-deployment stress-testing resource with 300 cases spanning misinformation, harmful output, bias, advertising, and indirect prompt injection.

The evaluation is unusually broad, covering 15 backend LLMs and three representative agent scaffolds. Three runs per case, cached authentic results, fixed adversarial content across agents, and ablations over result count, injection position, page length, timestamp, and website generator strengthen the empirical study.

The safety evaluator receives case-specific target consequences and checklists rather than relying on an unconstrained LLM judgment. Its validation on 200 responses reports 96–98% agreement with two human annotators, providing meaningful evidence that the principal ASR metric is reasonably reliable.

The results yield actionable findings: susceptibility differs greatly across models and risk categories; tool-calling and deeper research generally reduce attacks; misinformation remains especially difficult; and simple reminder prompting provides little protection. These observations make the benchmark potentially useful for development-time comparisons.

Simulation avoids manipulating live search rankings or exposing ordinary users to poisoned results. The ethics discussion recognizes reviewer exposure to disturbing material, and the limitations section appropriately acknowledges omitted proprietary systems, reliance on Google, benchmark scale, simulation-to-real transfer, and unmeasured operational cost.

The manuscript is generally well organized, visually legible, and substantially documented. It provides model and scaffold configurations, benchmark examples, generation and evaluation prompts, and an anonymous code and test-case repository.
weaknesses: The main ASRs should not be interpreted as estimates of real-world risk prevalence. Every retained case deliberately includes a highly relevant, synthetic unreliable page, whereas the paper does not estimate how often such a page would be retrieved, indexed, or ranked in deployment. The manuscript sometimes moves too freely from controlled vulnerability to claims that search agents broadly pose threats to users.

Benchmark selection is conditioned on a Qwen3-8B baseline succeeding under manipulation and not succeeding under benign retrieval. This is sensible for finding actionable failures, but it creates a deliberately attackable set, biases results toward that baseline and related behaviors, and limits claims about representative safety. Evaluation on an unfiltered random set or a separately generated holdout would clarify generalization.

The two motivating in-the-wild studies are under-validated. The reported 4.3% content-farm prevalence is based on GPT-4.1 classification without a human-validated sample, while the healthcare experiment reports 46 changed answers and only qualitatively states that “most” became riskier. Exact human annotation procedures, agreement, and risk counts are missing.

The helpfulness conclusions are not adequately supported. Helpfulness is judged solely by GPT-4.1-mini without human validation or reference answers, despite factual accuracy being part of its rubric. Near-ceiling scores even for unsafe manipulated responses suggest the metric may primarily capture surface relevance. Thus the claimed safety-helpfulness Pareto relationship is much weaker than the ASR findings.

Safety-judge validation reports raw agreement but not chance-corrected agreement, class prevalence, per-risk error rates, or false-positive/false-negative rates. Its 200 examples cover only three models under the search-workflow scaffold, leaving uncertainty about transfer to reasoning models, deep-research outputs, and individual risk categories.

Comparisons among scaffolds are partly confounded by search budget and evidence volume: the deep-research scaffold obtains substantially more opportunities for independent retrieval and cross-checking. This supports the benefit of the complete system but does not isolate scaffold structure as the cause. Deep research is also tested on only five of the 15 models.

Several quantitative claims lack uncertainty estimates or paired significance tests. With only 60 cases per risk and three stochastic repetitions, confidence intervals would help distinguish meaningful model and scaffold differences. There is also a factual inconsistency in Section 4.1, which attributes an 85.0% search-workflow ASR to GPT-4.1-mini although Table 2 reports 90.5% for GPT-4.1-mini and 85.0% for GPT-4.1.

Exact reproduction may be difficult because the study relies on mutable proprietary APIs, live Google/Serper results, and Jina extraction. The paper says results are cached, but it is not explicit that all cached pages, generated unreliable pages, complete run outputs, and versioned API settings are released. Reproduction claims should distinguish exact replay from rerunning against current services.

Releasing detailed harmful-content and deceptive-site generation recipes has dual-use potential. The simulation design responsibly prevents live poisoning, but the ethics discussion could more directly assess misuse of the released generation assets and describe safeguards or a responsible-release strategy.

strengths: Soundness: SAFESEARCH is a coherent controlled red-teaming framework. Its paired benign/manipulated retrieval setup helps attribute failures to the injected source: Appendix Table 10 reports a mean benign ASR of only 0.81%, compared with much larger manipulated-condition ASRs. The integrity/attainability filtering, three repeated runs, cached authentic results, and fixed injected page across agents are sensible design choices.

Evaluation breadth: The study tests 300 cases across five materially different risks, 17 backend LLMs, and three search-agent scaffolds. Table 1 reveals large and practically informative differences across models, risks, and scaffolds; the very low ASRs of GPT-5 and Claude-Sonnet-4.5 relative to many older/open models show that the benchmark is not merely guaranteed to declare every system unsafe.

The ablations cover many important implementation choices, including injected-result position, result count, content length, injection round, timestamp, website generator, generator model, persuasiveness, and two baseline defenses. These analyses make the framework more credible and useful than a single fixed attack configuration.

The checklist-conditioned safety judge is substantially better validated than is typical for LLM-based evaluations. On 200 randomly sampled outputs, two human annotators and the GPT-4.1-mini judge jointly agree on 95% of examples, with pairwise agreement of 96–98%. Concrete per-case checklists also make the labeling target relatively transparent.

Significance: Search agents consuming open-web evidence are increasingly important, and the paper demonstrates a useful development-time testing tool that avoids manipulating a live search engine. Findings such as the weakness of reminder prompting, partial effectiveness of filtering, and improved resilience under richer research scaffolds are actionable.

Originality: While related to RAG poisoning, prompt injection, and prior web-search safety evaluations, the combination of benign queries, one simulated unreliable result, automated scenario/page/checklist generation, and cross-risk agent benchmarking constitutes a useful new synthesis.

Presentation: The main workflow and threat model are clearly explained, and the extensive appendix provides prompts, concrete test cases, agent outputs, configuration details, and limitations. Tables and figures are generally legible despite the large experimental matrix.

Ethics and limitations: Simulation avoids exposing real users to black-hat SEO or harmful pages. The paper explicitly discusses the simulation-to-real gap, proprietary-system exclusion, single-search-provider coverage, benchmark scale, efficiency omissions, harmful content, and annotator fatigue rather than concealing these limitations.
weaknesses: Soundness/external validity: ASR is conditional on a deliberately synthesized, highly relevant unreliable page being inserted into the retrieved context. The study does not estimate how often such a page would actually be indexed, ranked, fetched successfully, or shown for the corresponding benign query. Consequently, results support susceptibility under controlled exposure, but not broad statements about the prevalence or end-to-end risk of failures in deployed search agents. The paper sometimes blurs this distinction when concluding that search agents are generally 'highly vulnerable.'

The two in-the-wild observations do not adequately close this realism gap. The reported 4.3% content-farm rate is produced by an unvalidated single GPT-4.1 classifier over synthetic persona queries. For the 46/1,000 health-answer stance changes, the paper gives no quantitative breakdown of how many changes were unsafe, how many were caused by unreliable sources, or how manual judgments were performed. These observations are therefore suggestive rather than systematic evidence for the simulated threat's frequency or severity.

Benchmark selection is explicitly conditioned on defeating Qwen3-8B while not triggering it in the benign condition. This is reasonable for red-teaming, but it biases the dataset toward that model/scaffold's failure modes and makes ASR unsuitable as an absolute safety measure. The paper should quantify generator/filter selection effects, report performance on an independently sampled unfiltered set, and more consistently frame scores as stress-test results.

Statistical reporting is weak relative to the scale of the conclusions. The paper provides point estimates without confidence intervals, paired uncertainty estimates, or significance tests. Claims about stable rankings, risk-category differences, reasoning models being safer, and scaffold advantages can be affected by finite test-case sampling, repeated stochastic trials, and confounding between model families and reasoning status.

The scaffold comparison is incomplete and potentially confounded: deep research is evaluated with only five models, uses substantially more searches/context and different orchestration, and is then compared with the full workflow/tool-calling averages. Paired comparisons under matched models and compute budgets are needed before attributing improvements specifically to scaffold design or cross-validation.

The 200-example judge validation is not stratified by risk type, model, or positive/negative class, and reports only raw agreement—not class prevalence, sensitivity, specificity, kappa, or disagreement adjudication. Both annotators are authors following the benchmark-generated checklists, which may mask shared interpretation bias. This is important because the judge determines the primary outcome.

Helpfulness is judged solely by GPT-4.1-mini and is not human-validated. Moreover, the paper describes the construct as perceived usefulness/plausibility, while Prompt 9 explicitly asks the judge to consider accuracy. This ambiguity makes conclusions that safety and helpfulness improve simultaneously, or are not in tension, insufficiently supported—especially when manipulated responses can appear polished while being false.

Originality is meaningful but moderate. The core ingredients—synthetic poisoning, indirect prompt injection, LLM-generated red-team cases, rubric-based judging, and simulated agent evaluation—are established individually. The distinction from the closest web-search and RAG-poisoning studies is discussed largely at a conceptual level and would benefit from direct empirical comparison with their benchmarks or methods.

Reproducibility is only partial. Prompts and many configurations are documented, but exact reproduction depends on changing proprietary models, live Google/Serper and Jina services, and generated/cached artifacts. The manuscript's code-release sentence has no visible repository link, and it omits uncertainty-producing details such as exact API model snapshots and complete cost/compute accounting. Releasing the cached results, generated pages, raw outputs, seeds, and evaluator labels is essential.

Ethics are handled responsibly overall, but release of detailed harmful-page generation guidelines and unsafe examples creates some dual-use risk. The impact statement asserts permitted API/code use and harm avoidance but does not describe release gating, misuse safeguards, or a concrete protocol for handling hazardous generated content. This is not an acceptance-blocking issue, but deserves a more operational treatment.

Presentation contains several overstatements and small inconsistencies: identifying failures provides evidence of an upper conditional failure rate rather than a 'lower bound of safety'; causal language about real-world danger exceeds the simulated evidence; and some figure references and model-detail tables appear inconsistent. Tightening these claims would materially improve the paper.

strengths: The paper addresses an important safety problem: search agents must reason over open-web evidence whose reliability is not controlled by the agent developer. The distinction from conventional static-corpus RAG is useful.

SAFESEARCH is a coherent automated pipeline combining scenario generation, synthetic unreliable pages, differential filtering, and checklist-based evaluation. Evaluating 300 retained cases across five risks, 17 models, and three scaffolds provides unusually broad empirical coverage.

The experiments include useful controls and ablations: benign versus manipulated retrieval, injection position and round, result count, token limits, timestamps, website/test generators, and two baseline defenses. The near-zero benign ASR in Table 10 supports a causal effect of the injected document within this simulation.

The finding that scaffold design matters in addition to the backend model is practically useful. Tool-calling and deep-research scaffolds generally lower ASR, and the results identify misinformation as particularly difficult.

The paper is generally well organized and clearly describes the threat model, prompts, and evaluation pipeline. It also acknowledges limitations involving proprietary agents, search-service coverage, benchmark scale, efficiency, and simulation-to-reality transfer.

The authors avoid manipulating live search rankings, reducing direct harm to external users. The impact statement also recognizes annotator exposure and the potentially offensive nature of some examples.
weaknesses: The central validity problem is selection on attack success. Cases are retained only when an injected page makes Qwen3-8B fail while the corresponding benign run does not; retention is as low as 6.8–6.9% for two categories. Consequently, reported ASRs measure transfer on an adversarially selected set, not the prevalence or typical severity of failures from ordinary unreliable search results. Headline conclusions such as agents being “highly vulnerable” and the 90.5% result are insufficiently qualified.

The simulation is not validated against the real distribution of unreliable web content. Injected pages are explicitly designed to be highly plausible, authoritative, query-specific, current, and sufficient to induce a predetermined consequence. Appending their full synthetic content to authentic results bypasses whether such a page would be indexed, ranked, extracted, and presented similarly in practice. The two motivating observations do not close this gap: the 4.3% content-farm estimate relies on an unvalidated GPT-4.1 classifier, while the health study reports only 46 stance changes and gives no precise count, annotation protocol, or agreement statistics for how many were unsafe.

Benchmark construction can distort model comparisons. Filtering on Qwen3-8B failures favors cases transferable from that model, while o4-mini generates cases and GPT-4.1-mini generates pages and judges outputs. Potential generator/evaluator family effects are not adequately separated. There is no independently sampled, unfiltered test set for estimating these biases.

The evaluator validation is inadequate for the breadth of the benchmark. It covers 200 outputs from only three models using one scaffold, reports raw agreement rather than confusion matrices, precision/recall, prevalence-adjusted statistics, or risk-wise results, and uses two authors rather than independent annotators. This does not justify applying one GPT-4.1-mini judge to all models, scaffolds, and risk categories, especially when the checklist is described as “not strict.”

Several comparative claims lack statistical support. The paper provides no confidence intervals, uncertainty estimates, or paired tests despite stochastic trials and repeated use of the same 300 generated cases. Claims that reasoning models are safer, rankings are stable, or particular scaffolds improve safety are therefore descriptive and may also be confounded by different tool-use behavior, answer length, safety tuning, and search frequency.

The helpfulness analysis is weak. A single LLM judges plausibility/usefulness without reference answers, although its prompt also asks about accuracy. High helpfulness for confidently fabricated responses is therefore difficult to interpret, and it does not establish the claimed safety–helpfulness trade-off or simultaneous improvement.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The manuscript says code and data are open-sourced, but the stated release location is blank. Reproducing results also requires proprietary model versions, Serper/Google results, Jina extraction, and cached webpages that are not demonstrably supplied. Appendix Table 6 is inconsistent with Table 1, listing models such as Qwen3-30B-A3B and LLaMA-3.3-70B that are not evaluated while omitting evaluated variants such as Kimi-K2 and Qwen3-235B-A22B-2507.

The limitations section is candid but does not acknowledge the most consequential limitation: success-conditioned sampling prevents ASR from being interpreted as a real-world risk rate. Some discussion instead speculates that proprietary systems are unlikely to be immune without evidence.

The release has meaningful dual-use risk because it includes detailed recipes for generating authoritative-looking misinformation, biased material, harmful instructions, and prompt injections. Simulation avoids harm during experimentation, but placing offensive examples in an appendix and stating benign intent do not address misuse of the released generators and dataset; a release-risk analysis or tiered/redacted release plan is missing.

Overall, the work contains a potentially useful stress-testing framework, but the paper substantially overinterprets a synthetic, success-filtered benchmark. Correcting the claims, adding an unfiltered and externally validated evaluation set, validating realism and judges more rigorously, and supplying complete artifacts would require major revision.

strengths: Soundness: The threat model is clearly specified, and the controlled comparison with versus without one injected unreliable result supports a causal claim about agent susceptibility. Benign-condition ASR averages only 0.81%, while manipulated-condition ASRs are often much higher. Significance: Safety under unreliable web evidence is important for increasingly deployed search agents. The evaluation is unusually broad, covering 300 cases, five risk categories, three scaffolds, and 17 backend models; the large model- and scaffold-dependent differences provide actionable guidance.

Originality: The individual ingredients—generated adversarial content, differential testing, LLM judges, and prompt-injection evaluation—are established, but their integration into an automated, multi-risk search-agent red-teaming framework is a useful and reasonably original system contribution.

Evaluation quality: The paper validates its checklist-assisted judge on 200 responses, reporting 95% unanimous agreement and 96–98% pairwise human/judge agreement. Three runs per case, cached search results, defense baselines, and extensive configuration ablations further strengthen the evidence.

Presentation, limitations, and ethics: The manuscript is polished and well organized, with extensive appendices containing prompts, examples, model settings, and limitations. It appropriately acknowledges simulation-to-real gaps, proprietary-agent exclusion, single-search-provider coverage, benchmark scale, and omitted efficiency costs. Simulation avoids harmful manipulation of live search rankings.
weaknesses: The headline ASRs should not be interpreted as estimates of real-world failure prevalence. Cases are generated for a target consequence and retained only when Qwen3-8B fails under manipulation but succeeds in the benign condition. This creates a deliberately enriched challenge set and selection bias toward that baseline’s vulnerabilities; model rankings and statements such as agents being “easily misled” therefore require more careful qualification.

Realism remains insufficiently validated. The injected pages are produced from detailed target-consequence instructions emphasizing plausibility and credibility, then inserted directly into search results. No quantitative human study assesses whether these pages resemble naturally occurring web content, and no safe observational experiment estimates how often comparable pages are actually retrieved. Position, length, and timestamp ablations do not fully close this simulation-to-real gap.

The evaluator validation is encouraging but limited: both annotators are authors, only 200 responses from three search-workflow models are sampled, and results are reported as raw agreement without per-risk confusion matrices, confidence intervals, or chance-corrected agreement. This leaves uncertainty about rare-category errors and generalization to tool-calling and deep-research outputs.

Statistical reporting is weak for the scale of the claims. The paper reports point estimates averaged over three stochastic runs but gives no uncertainty intervals, paired tests, or variance analyses. Consequently, small differences between models, scaffolds, timestamps, and defenses cannot be judged reliably.

Reproducibility details contain inconsistencies: Table 6 lists models not present in the main evaluation and omits some that are present, including Kimi-K2 and the evaluated Qwen3-235B-A22B-2507 variant. Reproduction also depends on mutable proprietary APIs, live search, and unspecified cached result artifacts; the manuscript’s visible code-release location is incomplete.

The ethics discussion handles direct experimental harm well but gives little attention to dual-use risks from releasing generators, prompts, and realistic deceptive webpages. A concrete release policy or abuse-mitigation plan would improve the treatment of this concern.
